opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the big thing is that a tool description is basically a prompt, and people tend to forget that. They'll write a function signature and a one-line docstring and expect the model to just figure out how to use it well. But think about how you'd onboard a new engineer to an internal tool. You wouldn't just hand them the type signature. You'd say, "Here's how you'd actually call this. Here's a common case, here's an edge case, and here's the mistake everybody makes the first time."

Examples do a few things really well. First, they disambiguate. A parameter called `path` could be relative or absolute, a file or a directory, with or without a trailing slash. You can write a paragraph explaining that, or you can show one example call and the model immediately gets it. Models are incredibly good at pattern-matching off concrete examples, often better than they are at following abstract rules.

Second, they show intent, not just syntax. A good example says, "When you're in this situation, this is the call you'd make." That teaches the model when to reach for the tool, which is half the battle. A lot of tool-use failures aren't malformed calls. They're the model picking the wrong tool or not using a tool when it should.

The caveat is that examples are really strong signals, so the model can overfit to them. If every example uses the same kind of input, you'll see the model copy that pattern even when it doesn't fit. So you want a few diverse examples that cover the space, not five variations of the same thing.

When we were building our coding agent for SWE-bench, a huge amount of the work went into the tools rather than the overall prompt: making the descriptions really clear, adding examples, and even changing the tool interfaces so they were harder to misuse. For instance, requiring absolute paths so the model couldn't get confused about which directory it was in. I think of it as prompt engineering for the agent-computer interface. You should spend as much care on it as you would on a human-facing API, maybe more, because the model can't walk over to your desk and ask what you meant.

r001.rationale: The response says examples can clarify tool use better than abstract rules or paragraphs, but it does not compare a common example with reading an exhaustive list of tool options.

r002.rationale: It compares writing tool guidance to onboarding a new engineer, then explains how examples help models too, communicating that human-useful documentation can also help language models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we learned pretty painfully while building out the tool ecosystem for Claude Code. The intuition people usually start with is that a tool description is like an API spec—you list the parameters, their types, what the function returns, and you're done. And that's necessary, but it turns out it's nowhere near sufficient.

The reason is that a model has to make a bunch of judgment calls that a schema just doesn't encode. When should I reach for this tool versus a similar one? What does a "good" input actually look like in practice? What are the common pitfalls? If you've got a search tool and a file-read tool, the type signature doesn't tell you that the search tool is the thing you want when you don't know where something lives, and the read tool is for when you do. An example does that immediately—it shows the model the situation and the right response together, so it's learning the pattern rather than reconstructing it from first principles every time.

There's also a thing where models, like humans, are much better at pattern-matching from a concrete instance than from an abstract description. If I tell you "the query parameter accepts a regex," that's true, but if I show you two or three realistic queries—including one with escaping that trips people up—you're going to use it correctly far more often. We saw measurable drops in tool-call errors just from adding a few well-chosen examples to descriptions, without touching the model at all.

And the last piece is that examples let you encode negative guidance in a way that feels natural. You can show "here's when you'd use this" and implicitly "here's when you wouldn't," which is hard to say crisply in prose without the description turning into a wall of caveats. So honestly, I think of good examples as the cheapest lever you have for improving agent reliability—way cheaper than fine-tuning, and often more effective than rewriting the system prompt.

r001.rationale: The response says parameter lists and schemas are necessary but insufficient, and that concrete usage examples teach the model the pattern and help it use tools correctly.

r002.rationale: It explicitly compares models with humans, saying both learn better from concrete examples than abstract descriptions.

astra-6.text: Usage examples make the intended behavior concrete. You can describe all the arguments to a tool, but there can still be ambiguity about how they fit together or what a valid call looks like. An example shows the model, “In this situation, here’s how you use it.” Models are very good at picking up patterns from context, so a couple of representative examples can communicate things that would take a lot of prose to explain.

r001.rationale: It contrasts listing all tool arguments with representative examples that show valid use and communicate patterns more clearly, presenting examples as a better way to learn how to use the tool.

r002.rationale: It explains why examples help language models, but does not say that documentation useful to humans is also useful to models.

sol-6.1.text: Usage examples show the model what a successful tool call actually looks like. You can describe all the arguments in prose, but an example makes the conventions concrete: how to format a query, which arguments to combine, or when to use an optional parameter. It’s essentially few-shot prompting inside the tool description. That’s especially useful when the schema tells you what’s valid but doesn’t tell you what’s useful.
